h: Trails from the door and sights up the glen
p: You don't have to drive anywhere to start walking. Several waymarked trails set off from the visitor centre itself, including the short route to Signal Rock, a wooded knoll that tradition links with the signal for the 1692 massacre, and pleasant woodland walks along the River Coe. They're great for families and anyone who wants a taste of the glen without tackling the mountains.

In the village of Glencoe, just down the road, Glencoe Lochan is a peaceful little loch surrounded by woodland trails, created by Lord Strathcona in the nineteenth century. It's a calm spot for a stroll, with reflections of the mountains in the water on still days. The Glencoe Folk Museum, in a group of thatched cottages, has a charming collection about local life.

Head east along the A82 and the scenery just keeps getting better. The Three Sisters, a trio of huge ridges, tower over the road, and there are viewpoints and lay-bys where you can pull in safely. Further on, the pyramid of Buachaille Etive Mòr guards the entrance to the glen, one of the most photographed mountains in Scotland. Beyond it, Rannoch Moor opens out, wild and empty. Glen Etive, a single-track road winding south-west, featured in the James Bond film Skyfall.

At Glencoe Mountain, a chairlift runs up the hillside for big views even if you're not a skier. Fort William, at the foot of Ben Nevis, is about half an hour's drive north for food, shops and more adventure.
